summary: Surveys commonly used network security protocols, looking at how they interact with applications and transport protocols. It supplements work to define and catalog Transport Services by describing the interfaces needed to add security protocols. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary:
Securing a connection means running one protocol on top of another. This RFC looks at the common security protocols, the transport each one needs underneath it, and the choices each one offers to the program using it.

The result is a reference for anyone designing a single interface that can hide whichever security protocol is in use.

questions: how do security protocols interact with transport services
what are the interfaces of security protocols
what is the difference between tls and quic
how does ipv4 relate to security protocols
what interfaces does tls expose to an application
which security protocols run over udp
subtitle: How the common ways of securing a connection fit with the transport below them and the application above them.

tldr.problem: Building a secure connection means putting a security protocol on top of a transport protocol, and the two have to fit. Different protocols need different things from the transport, and expose different things to the application.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogues ten security protocols, groups them by where they sit in the stack, lists which transport each one needs, and tabulates the thirteen interfaces each one offers to an application.
tldr.outcome: The survey is a guide for designing a common interface, so that software can adopt new secure transports without rewriting its application. It deliberately does not recommend one protocol over another.

facts.label: Protocols needing a reliable byte stream

today: RFC 8922 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It is a survey, not a specification: it proposes no changes to any protocol and recommends none over another. Its purpose is to support the work on a common interface for transport services, and it notes that a separate document would be needed to survey the privacy features of the protocols it covers.

sections.title: What This Survey Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
Transport protocols and the features they offer have already been catalogued in RFC 8095. This document complements that work on the security side. It surveys the network security protocols that are commonly used or otherwise notable, and identifies the interfaces between them, the transport protocols below them, and the applications above them.

The protocols examined are TLS, DTLS, IETF QUIC, Google QUIC (gQUIC), tcpcrypt, IPsec, Secure RTP with DTLS, WireGuard, CurveCP and MinimaLT. For each one there is a short description, then Section 4 covers the transport dependencies and Section 5 the application interfaces.

The reason to do this is a common interface. One goal of the Transport Services work is to define a single interface for using transport protocols, so that software can adopt a new protocol with a similar feature set without changes. Knowing what a security protocol needs from the transport shows which transports are usable beneath it. A protocol that expects a reliable stream of bytes, such as TLS, restricts the choice to transports that offer one.

Defining the interfaces that security protocols offer to applications matters for the same reason. Many security protocols let the application take part in checking who the peer is, so any interface for a secure transport has to allow that during connection setup.

The RFC is careful about what it does not do. It is not a goal to let software switch automatically between security protocols, because even between versions they differ in guarantees and weaknesses. Nor is it a goal to find one common representation of peer identity or authentication, since different protocols mean these differently. Protocols that add nothing new are left out: SSH, GRE, L2TP and ALTS are omitted because they offer no distinctive interfaces. Authentication-only protocols are also omitted, including the TCP Authentication Option and the IPsec Authentication Header, because neither has general use and neither offers confidentiality or privacy protection. Only point-to-point protocols are covered.
sections.plainLanguage:
Secure connections are built in layers, and each layer expects something different from the one below.

This RFC gathers ten widely used security protocols and records what each needs from the transport and what each offers to the program above it. It does not tell you which one to use.

sections.title: The Words the Survey Uses
sections.content:
A transport feature is an end-to-end capability the transport layer offers an application, such as confidentiality, reliable delivery, ordered delivery, and whether the data is a stream of bytes or a set of messages. A transport service is a set of those features, not tied to any particular framing on the wire. A transport protocol is an implementation that provides one or more transport services using a specific framing and header format.

A transport services system is the software component that exposes an interface to different transport services to an application. An application is the entity using a transport protocol for end-to-end delivery, which may itself be an upper layer protocol or a tunnel encapsulation.

A security protocol is a defined network protocol that implements one or more security features, such as authentication, encryption, key generation, session resumption and privacy. It may be used alongside a transport protocol, and in combination with other security protocols.

The rest of the terms describe the pieces of a secure connection. A handshake protocol lets peers validate each other and establish shared cryptographic context. A record is a framed protocol message, and a record protocol divides data into manageable blocks and protects them using that shared context. A session is an ephemeral security association between applications. A connection is the shared state of two or more endpoints that persists across the messages exchanged between them; a connection is a transient participant of a session, and a session generally lasts between connection instances. A peer is an endpoint party to a session, and the client is the peer that initiates it while the server responds.
sections.plainLanguage: Several of these words are easy to mix up, so the RFC defines them precisely. The important distinction is between a session, which is the overall secure relationship, and a connection, which is one piece of it that can be replaced.

sections.title: The Protocols, Grouped by Where They Sit
sections.content:
The protocols are grouped by their position in the stack, because that decides which part of a packet they protect. The groups are the generic application payload, the payload of a specific application protocol, both the application payload and the transport headers, and the whole IP packet.

Not every protocol fits neatly into one group, because some can be used in different ways or alongside other protocols. A common reason is that channel security protocols usually have two parts: a handshake protocol that negotiates parameters, authenticates the endpoints and establishes shared keys, and a record protocol that encrypts traffic with the keys the handshake produced. In tcpcrypt the two are tightly integrated. In IPsec they are separate protocols, because AH and ESP are record protocols that can take keys from the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2), from other handshake protocols, or from manual configuration. Some protocols can also be used in different ways: TLS has an integrated handshake and record protocol, but TLS or DTLS can also negotiate keys for another protocol, as in DTLS-SRTP, and a handshake protocol can be used with a separate record layer, as in QUIC.

In the application payload group, TLS establishes a secure session between two endpoints and prevents eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery. Its handshake authenticates peers, negotiates options such as cryptographic algorithms and derives session keying material; its record protocol marshals and, once the handshake has progressed far enough, encrypts the data. DTLS is TLS adapted for unreliable datagram transports such as UDP, and keeps the same guarantees except for order protection and replay resistance.

Secure RTP (SRTP) is a profile for RTP that gives confidentiality, message authentication and replay protection to RTP and RTCP packets. It supplies only a record layer, so it needs a separate handshake. The usual one is DTLS in the form of DTLS-SRTP, an extension that negotiates SRTP as the record layer and describes how to export keys. ZRTP is an alternative, performing a Diffie-Hellman key exchange on the media path to produce the shared secret from which the SRTP master key and salt are derived.

In the transport-layer group, IETF QUIC is a standards-track transport protocol over UDP, loosely based on Google's earlier gQUIC. The QUIC transport layer provides confidentiality and integrity but needs a separate handshake, for which a mapping of TLS 1.3 has been specified. gQUIC itself is a UDP-based multiplexed streaming protocol designed and deployed by Google after experience with SPDY, with tightly integrated security and data transport. tcpcrypt is a lightweight TCP extension offering opportunistic encryption; its session ID can be used for further application-level authentication, and without that it is open to active attacks. MinimaLT is a UDP-based transport security protocol offering confidentiality, mutual authentication, denial-of-service prevention and connection mobility, and it reuses a variant of TCP's congestion control. CurveCP is a UDP-based transport security protocol built entirely on public key algorithms, and it provides its own reliability for application data.

In the packet group, IKEv2 and ESP together form the modern IPsec suite, encrypting and authenticating IP packets either for tunnels or for direct transport connections, and separating key generation from transport encryption. WireGuard is an IP-layer alternative to IPsec for certain cases, encapsulating IP datagrams between peers over UDP. Instead of Public Key Infrastructure, it authenticates peers with pre-shared public keys delivered out of band, each bound to one or more IP addresses, and it offers no extensibility, negotiation or cryptographic agility. OpenVPN is another alternative to IPsec, designed to be simple to configure and to work over several transports; it encapsulates IP packets or Ethernet frames in a secure tunnel over UDP or TCP and can use TLS or pre-shared keys for key establishment.
sections.plainLanguage:
The protocols fall into four families, depending on how much of the packet they protect: just the data, the data plus the transport headers, or the entire IP packet.

Most of them are built from two halves. One half sets up the keys and checks who is on the other end. The other half uses those keys to protect the data that follows.

sections.title: What Each Protocol Needs From the Transport
sections.content:
Across all the protocols, the main dependency on the transport is how data is presented: either an endless stream of bytes, or framed messages. Most protocols that rely on the transport for framing are built to run over a transport that provides framing itself, such as UDP, but some also define how their messages can be framed over a byte-stream transport.

Only TLS and tcpcrypt need a reliable, in-order stream of bytes, which in practice means TCP.

The rest depend on the transport to frame their messages, and are built to run over UDP with no reliability requirement. Running them over a reliable transport will not break anything, but can stack reliability on top of reliability when the security protocol is carrying other transport traffic.

Some of those datagram protocols also have well-defined mappings for running over a byte-stream transport such as TCP: DTLS when it acts as the handshake protocol for SRTP, ZRTP, SRTP itself, and IPsec.

One protocol has a direct dependency on a specific transport feature. tcpcrypt is designed to run on TCP and uses the TCP Encryption Negotiation Option (TCP-ENO) to negotiate its protocol support.

Three protocols provide transport functionality as well as security: QUIC, CurveCP and MinimaLT. They depend on a framed protocol such as UDP, but they add their own layers of reliability and other transport features. An application using one of them therefore cannot separate the security from the transport functionality.
sections.plainLanguage:
Most of these protocols need a transport that keeps message boundaries, such as UDP. Only TLS and tcpcrypt insist on a reliable, ordered byte stream.

Three of them, QUIC, CurveCP and MinimaLT, mix the two jobs: they are transports and security systems at once.

sections.title: The Interfaces Exposed to Applications
sections.content:
The interfaces are split into three groups, following the conventions of the Transport Services work. Not every protocol supports every interface.

Pre-connection interfaces configure the security protocol before a handshake begins. There are six of them. Identities and Private Keys lets the application supply its identity, credentials such as certificates, private keys, or a way to reach them. Supported Algorithms lets the application choose the key exchange, signature and ciphersuite algorithms. Extensions lets it enable or configure extensions to be negotiated, such as Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN). Session Cache Management lets the application save and retrieve session state, such as tickets and keying material, so that a session can be resumed. Authentication Delegation gives the application access to a separate module that performs authentication, for example using the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP). Pre-Shared Key Import lets the handshake protocol or the application supply pre-shared keys for use with a peer.

Connection interfaces apply during the handshake. Identity Validation is the check of the peer's identity, which the security protocol may offload or perform transparently. Source Address Validation is where the handshake interacts with the transport or the application to check the address of the remote peer that sent data, which involves a cookie exchange to avoid denial-of-service attacks. Protocols that depend on TCP are omitted from this list because they perform it implicitly.

Post-connection interfaces apply once the connection is up. Connection Termination lets the security protocol be told to tear down its connection and session state, which some protocols need to stop an attacker terminating an underlying insecure connection to end the session. Key Update updates keying material, either on request from the application or when the record protocol reports that a key is expiring. Shared Secret Key Export produces shared secrets for application-specific uses. Key Expiration is the signal that keys are reaching a time-based or use-based limit, often between the record layer and the handshake layer. Mobility Events signal that the record protocol is moving to another transport or interface, which can reset address and state validation and cause a new Connection Identifier to be used.

Table 1 of the RFC then records which protocol exposes which interface. TLS, DTLS, QUIC, MinimaLT and IPsec are the broadest. CurveCP offers very little: identities and keys, identity validation, and mobility events. WireGuard offers identities and keys, pre-shared key import, identity validation, source address validation and mobility events, but no algorithm choice and no termination.
sections.plainLanguage:
An application talks to the security protocol through a small set of controls. Some are set up before the connection, some act during the handshake, and some act afterwards.

Which controls exist varies a lot between protocols, and the RFC's final table records the differences.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC makes no claim about security or privacy beyond what the protocols it surveys already guarantee. It does not propose changes to any of them and does not recommend one over another.

Two limitations apply to every protocol in the survey. Metadata can leak through timing side channels and traffic analysis, which can compromise any of them. An application using these interfaces should take such limits into account when choosing an implementation.

On privacy, the RFC deliberately leaves the analysis out, on the grounds that a survey of privacy features, or the lack of them, deserves a document of its own. In general, encryption improves privacy by reducing what leaks, but different amounts of metadata stay in the clear. Client and server certificates, for example, are sent in cleartext in TLS 1.2, RFC 5246, and are encrypted in TLS 1.3, RFC 8446.
sections.plainLanguage: The survey makes no promises beyond what each protocol already guarantees. Encryption does not remove every trace: timing and traffic analysis still leak information, and some metadata stays in the clear.
